entry.title: So you wrote a Ring adapter
entry.content:
A Ring adapter is the easiest thing you will ever write. It is also one of the hardest, and the gap between those two sentences is the whole story. I spent the last while closing that gap — the thing that came out of it is called enso, a zero-dependency HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and WebSocket server for Ring — so let me walk you from the easy version to the one you can actually point at the internet, one missed corner at a time.

Here is the easy version. You have seen it, you have probably written it.

(defn serve [handler port]
  (let [server (ServerSocket. port)]
    (future
      (loop []
        (let [sock (.accept server)]
          (future
            (with-open [s sock]
              (let [req  (parse-request (.getInputStream s))
                    resp (handler req)]
                (write-response (.getOutputStream s) resp)))))
        (recur)))
    server))

Accept a socket, parse a request, call the handler, write the response. A thread per connection. On JDK 21 you make those virtual threads and it even scales. curl localhost:8080 returns your {:status 200 :body "hello"}. The README example passes. Ship it.

Unsurprisingly, it is completely broken. Not in a "needs polish" way — in a "do not put this on a network" way please. Let me show you.

Where does the body end?

parse-request read the headers. Did it read the body? A GET has none, so your tests pass. A POST with Content-Length: 1048576 has a megabyte the handler may or may not read. If your handler ignores :body — plenty do — those bytes are still sitting in the socket when you go to write the response and read the next request. Now you are parsing a request body as if it were a request line. On a keep-alive connection you have desynchronised yourself from the client, and every response after is garbage.

So you need a real framing layer: Content-Length and chunked transfer-encoding, the knowledge that HEAD and 204 and 304 carry no body regardless of their headers, and a rule for what happens to a body the handler never read (you drain it, within a bound — more on bounds later). None of this is in the forty lines. All of it is mandatory.

The client that says nothing

Open a socket to the easy version. Send nothing. parse-request blocks on a read that never returns. That is one virtual thread gone. Cheap, sure. Now open ten thousand of them, each dribbling one byte every twenty-nine seconds — slow enough that no single read times out, because there is no timeout. This is slowloris, it is from 2009, and your forty lines have no answer to it.

A real adapter has a small forest of clocks, and they are all different:

  • a handshake deadline (TLS can stall too),
  • a header deadline — the whole request head, wall-clock, from its first byte, because a per-read timeout resets every time one byte arrives,
  • a read timeout between body chunks,
  • an idle timeout between requests on a kept-alive connection,
  • and a minimum data rate — Kestrel uses 240 bytes/second after a 5 second grace, and so, it turns out, do I — because a client sending one byte every twenty-nine seconds technically keeps making progress forever.

The easy version has none of these. Each one is a real decision with a real default, and getting the defaults wrong is its own bug.

The two parsers that disagree

Send this:

POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: x
Content-Length: 6
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0

GET /admin HTTP/1.1
...

Your naive parser picks one of Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding and moves on. The proxy in front of you picks the other. Now the two of you disagree about where the first request ends and the second begins, and I have smuggled a second request past whatever the proxy thought it was authorising. This is request smuggling, and it is not a parsing nit — it is a security boundary that exists between your parser and someone else's.

So: reject a message with both framing headers. Reject duplicate Content-Length. Reject a bare LF line ending where the spec wants CRLF. Reject obs-fold — the obsolete trick of continuing a header value onto the next line by starting it with a space, which two parsers routinely disagree about. Reject a chunk size that overflows a long. Validate the request target and the Host authority. Every one of these is a line in an RFC and a CVE in someone's tracker, and "I'll be lenient, it's friendlier" is exactly how you end up on the wrong side of one.

Closing is harder than opening

Your handler returns a 400. You write it and close the socket. Clean, right?

Except the client was still uploading its body when you decided to reject it. There are unread bytes in the kernel's receive buffer. On most operating systems, closing a socket with unread input sends a TCP RST — the abrupt "forget this connection ever existed" reset — and a reset blows away the send buffer too, including the 400 you just wrote. The client never sees your error. It sees a connection reset and has no idea why.

The fix is counterintuitive: to close correctly you close slower. You shut down the write side, then keep reading and discarding input until the peer closes or a short deadline passes, so your response drains out before the socket goes away. There's a TLS twist too. An HTTP/1.0 response with no Content-Length is delimited by the connection closing, so the receiver can't otherwise tell "body ended here" from "body got cut off." TLS normally ends with a close_notify alert meaning "this was a clean, complete shutdown" — so when you're abandoning a body mid-stream, you deliberately close without that alert, which is exactly the signal that lets the client tell a truncated body from a finished one. These are the kind of corners you only find by watching a real client get a reset where you sent a response.

Then you add HTTP/2 and the threat model changes

One TCP connection is now many streams. Most of the above still applies, per stream, but there is a new category: the connection is a shared resource a single client can turn against you.

The famous one is rapid reset — CVE-2023-44487, the one that took out a chunk of the internet in 2023. A client opens a stream, you start doing work, the client immediately sends RST_STREAM. Repeat as fast as the wire allows. Each reset is cheap for the client and not cheap for you. There is a sequel, MadeYouReset, where the client doesn't send RST_STREAM at all — it sends a frame that's malformed in just the right way (a stray WINDOW_UPDATE, say) so that you, the server, are forced to reset the stream in response. The work still happened, but the reset came from your side, so your own rapid-reset counter never trips — unless you count the resets you initiate on the client's behalf too, which is the sort of thing you only think of after reading the first CVE very carefully.

So you add reset accounting, a cap on CONTINUATION floods (an unending run of header-continuation frames that stretches one request's headers forever), empty- DATA flood detection (zero-length DATA frames that cost the attacker nothing and you a syscall each), flow-control-window bookkeeping that survives a stream being reset mid-frame, yadda-yadda... The handler still just returns a map. All of this lives underneath.

And now the hard one

Here is the question I underestimated the longest, and it is so easy to state that it hides how hard it is:

When a client sends data faster than your handler reads it, where does the data go?

The forty-line version has an answer by accident: into an unbounded buffer, until you run out of memory. One connection, one OutOfMemory, whole server down. So you add a cap — a maximum number of buffered bytes — and feel good.

Now the cap fills up. A client is uploading a 2 GB body to a handler that reads slowly, or doesn't read at all, and you have hit your buffer limit. What do you do?

The obvious thing — and I mean obvious, I did it, most servers I looked at do some version of it — is to stop reading from that socket and let the clocks from earlier run. Eventually the minimum-data-rate or read timeout fires and you return a 408 Request Timeout. Problem solved.

Except you just lied to the client. You stopped reading, to protect your memory. The client was sending at a perfectly good rate the whole time; it is blocked because your receive window is closed, which it is closed because you chose not to drain it. Then you timed the client out for a stall you created and blamed it in the logs. I know this happens because I ran a multi-hour soak with a deliberately tiny memory budget and watched a pile of 408s go to clients that had done nothing wrong.

The honest version is more work, and some accounting, and it is the part of enso I spent the most time getting right.

  • One budget for the whole server. Not a per-connection buffer — a single pool of "bytes we are willing to hold on behalf of peers," shared across HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and WebSocket, enforced by back-pressure.
  • Fair shares. Under pressure, one connection cannot hold more than its slice (the budget divided by the connections actually holding bytes), so one fat uploader can't freeze everyone else's uploads.
  • A floor, so the budget limits growth, never progress. Every connection may always hold a small amount — the same 64 KB that HTTP/2 hands every stream as its default window before anyone configures anything — so an upload on a connection under its floor keeps moving even when the global budget is exhausted. You throttle; you never fully stall.
  • Clocks that only count time the client could have used. This is the fix for the lie. While the server is the one withholding reads — a receive window it has deliberately closed, a stream it has chosen not to drain — the read timeout and the data-rate clock for that body are paused. They resume when the server starts reading again. A client is only ever timed out for a stall it actually caused.

That last rule sounds small and it took real work to get right across three protocols, because "the server is withholding" means something different in each: HTTP/2 it's a connection window we haven't replenished, HTTP/3 it's a stream the event loop isn't reading, WebSocket it's a message we've stopped pulling because the budget is full. Same principle, three mechanisms.

And the payoff is a property you can state in one sentence: **the server never blames a client for back-pressure the server applied.** Concretely: a client only ever gets a 408 Request Timeout when it actually went quiet — stopped sending, stalled below the data-rate floor, genuinely slow. A client that was sending as fast as the wire allowed, and only went idle because the server clamped its flow-control window to protect its own memory, never collects the blame for that pause. The timeout measures the client's behaviour, never the server's self-defence. That distinction doesn't exist in the forty-line version — it can't, because the forty-line version has no idea whether a silent socket is a slow client or a window it closed itself.

Not every server bothers to draw that line.

Doesn't all this blocking cost a thread?

Everything above is written in the blocking style the forty-line version started with: read, block, parse, call the handler, write, repeat. And the whole point of back-pressure is that it stops reading — a slow upload, or one the budget is throttling, is a connection sitting on a blocked read for a long time. On the classic thread-per-connection model that is exactly the disaster slowloris exploited: ten thousand slow connections, ten thousand parked OS threads, server dead.

The reason the parking isn't a disaster here is that the threads aren't OS threads. Each HTTP/1.1 connection, and each HTTP/2 stream, runs on its own virtual thread. A blocking read on a virtual thread unmounts it from its carrier — the parked upload becomes a continuation on the heap, a few hundred bytes, not an idle kernel thread. So a connection we've deliberately stopped reading from costs almost nothing to keep around, which is the whole trick: back-pressure that blocks is the single cheapest thing you can do to a virtual thread.

But notice this does not retroactively solve slowloris, and I don't want to pretend it does. Virtual threads take the thread-exhaustion vector off the table — ten thousand stalled connections are no longer ten thousand pinned OS threads. They're still ten thousand live connections, each holding a socket, a file descriptor and a little heap, forever, because the forty-line version never set a deadline. Cheap is not free, and unbounded times cheap is still dead. The thing that actually answers slowloris is the clock that eventually says "you've made no real progress, goodbye"; the virtual thread just makes waiting out that clock, for a legitimately slow client, affordable instead of fatal. The two sections aren't in tension — the thread model decides what idle waiting costs, the deadlines decide when waiting ends, and you need both.

The clocks don't cost a thread each either. Every handshake, header, idle and data-rate deadline across every connection and protocol lives in one hashed timing wheel on a single daemon thread; arming a timeout is appending to a bucket, not spawning anything.

HTTP/3 is the one that works the other way, and it's worth saying because it's the exception. Its I/O runs on a small fixed pool of event-loop threads — by default one per core — with every connection multiplexed across them and the kernel steering datagrams by connection id. There, "withholding" a stream isn't a blocked thread at all; it's the loop choosing not to drain that stream this tick and moving on to the next. Different shape, same result: the cost of holding a throttled peer is bounded and tiny, whether that peer is parked on a virtual thread or skipped by an event loop.

The moral, such as it is

The forty-line adapter isn't wrong because it's short. It's wrong because "serve a request" is a surface over a long tail of concerns — framing, timeouts, smuggling, resets, lingering close, back-pressure — that don't show up in the demo and all show up in production. "Simple", was never "few lines." It's each of those concerns handled once, cleanly, so that the person using it writes

(enso/run-server (fn [req] {:status 200 :body "hello"}) {:port 8080})

and none of it leaks out.

And that's the pitch. Not that it's fast, though it is.

And I have no illusion the list above is complete. Somewhere out there is a client, or a proxy, or a single malformed frame that I haven't thought of yet, and the day someone files the three-line repro for it is the day I learn about corner number N+1. Find it? Open an issue. I collect them.

entry.title: Init
entry.content:
So it seems it's the year of the blogs again. I figured it would be a good exercise to get back into it and share some of the things I experiment with, especially related to programming and surrounding topics.

A few words about me first for those who don't know who I am. I am a mid-century software engineer, in that soft spot between "experienced" and soon to be considered a fossil I suppose. I currently work for Exoscale, a European Cloud platform. Even though what I mention on this blog might occasionally refer to what I do at work indirectly, these are my words only.

One subject that has been occupying my mind quite a bit lately is complexity in software design in orgs with multiple dev teams. Don't leave just yet! So expect to see a bit of writing about this topic in the future.

I swear I won't bore about mono/mini/macro/ repos & the like.

I have a few other things in my bag such as various clojure related topics and subjects related to what I work on day to day, various types of orchestrators that power a cloud platform such as exoscale. I might also drop the occasional emacs discovery.

But for now I am just getting this bloging engine setup, courtesy of https://blog.michielborkent.nl/, and will iterate from there.

See you on the next one!
